title: ImageNet-trained CNNs are not biased towards texture: Revisiting feature re

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper describes a human experiment with 20 participants completing recognition trials with brief 200 ms image presentations and a 'not clear' button, but never states that the study received institutional review board (IRB) or ethics committee approval, nor that informed consent was obtained. Human subjects research in a scientific publication must include an ethics statement; its absence is a serious omission.

The bilateral filter parameter d differs between the validation in Table 2 (d=11, Param ID A) and the actual suppression used in the human experiment (d=12, described in Section 5.1). The validation results therefore do not exactly correspond to the transformation applied to human participants, undermining the claimed 'justification' of the chosen parameters.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.1 (human experiment design and comparison with models)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Human participants were allowed to press a 'not clear' button for unrecognizable stimuli, but the paper does not specify how these responses were treated when computing human accuracy. In contrast, models always produce a forced prediction. The lack of a matching evaluation protocol and the undisclosed treatment of 'not clear' responses make the comparative human–model accuracy and reliance profiles unreliable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, first bullet ('First, CV models are most reliant on local shape, especially when trained from scratch...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main paper only shows CV suppression curves for models initialized with ImageNet-pretrained weights (Figure 4 top row). No results for CV models trained from scratch are presented in the main figures or tables. The claim about from-scratch behaviour therefore lacks direct visible support in the paper.
